body_en:
This article is based on a video by Douyin creator Chaoge Talks Cars.

Listen up, young guys. Make good money — and buy yourself a good, expensive e-bike.

If you've saved up a hundred or two hundred thousand yuan, you're earning decent money, and you spend your days researching four-wheelers with their “fridge, big TV, and sofa seats,” agonizing over which model to buy — let me tell you, that thinking is dangerous. What you should really be researching is a high-end, quality electric bike.

How to Choose a High-End E-Bike

Don't think of an e-bike as a two- or three-thousand-yuan commuter. A high-end e-bike is a completely different animal.

TAILG, Luyuan, and Yadea all make serious high-end models, and so do Ninebot and Niu. Take Ninebot's FZ5110: a 48V 30Ah lithium battery, a claimed range of 100 kilometers — in practice you'll still get several dozen kilometers out of it, more than enough for a daily commute. Or Niu's NXT: superb handling, a low center of gravity, a rock-steady ride. Yadea's high-end models have bigger frames and can even carry a passenger in the back.

Other people spend two or three thousand yuan on an e-bike. You spend five or six thousand on a top-spec model, add a few accessories, and you're in for six or seven thousand all told. What you're buying is not the same thing at all.

Small Upgrades, a Completely Different Ride

Once you've got the bike, it's worth investing a little more. Most people won't spend the money — but it's money well spent.

Take the tires. The stock vacuum tires run about 90 or 100 yuan each. Swap in a pair of good Michelins — tires plus labor, six or seven hundred yuan for the pair. Michelin tires are softer, with lower rolling resistance, better range, and better shock absorption. Someone who bought a two-thousand-yuan e-bike would think spending another 600 on tires is absurd. But spend it, and it's worth every cent.

Or spend about 150 yuan on a decent extendable lumbar support, mounted on the back seat to brace your lower back. When you're young, your back never hurts, so you don't notice. But on a long ride — thirty kilometers or more — having that support makes a world of difference.

The Trap of Buying Your First Car

For an ordinary family, money doesn't come easy. And the car most people end up wanting is the classic trap: too good for the cheap ones, too broke for the ones you actually want.

Your parents scrimp and save and grit their teeth to hand you 50,000 yuan. But would you honestly be happy with a 50,000- or 70,000-yuan car? Of course not — you'd be looking at 150,000, at 200,000, at a Tesla, a Xiaomi SU7, a Fangchengbao, something like that. But you're fresh out into the world, just starting to earn. Keeping yourself fed is already an achievement.

So how does it usually end? Your parents put in 50,000 or 80,000, you take out a loan for the rest, grit your teeth, and stretch into a 100,000- or 200,000-yuan electric car. Let me be blunt: you're asking for trouble. The last thing you should buy is a car you can't afford.

An E-Bike and a Car Don't Cost the Same Kind of Money

Buy a high-end e-bike and there's no car loan, no gas, no maintenance, no hunting for parking. You don't lie awake worrying about it going out of date, getting scratched, or dropping in value the way you would with a 200,000-yuan EV. There's no mandatory annual insurance either — though if it makes you feel better, a third-party liability policy is cheap.

Other people spend their money on anxiety. You spend yours on freedom.

What If You Really Do Have 200,000 or 300,000 Yuan?

But Chaoge, what if I really do have the money — a real 200,000 or 300,000 yuan?

My friend, here's my advice: you're working away from home, and at your age, having 200,000 or 300,000 yuan to your name is seriously impressive — you're one in a million. That money wasn't earned back in some small county town; you earned it in a big city. So go rent a nicer apartment closer to the office. If you're going to spend, spend it there — not on a car.

Buy a car and you have to look after it every day: washing it, servicing it, paying tickets and insurance, finding parking, dealing with all the hassle — plus the risk of being on the road. Rent a place closer to work, buy a high-end e-bike, and that's what real comfort looks like.

Cash Is King: Money in Hand Changes You

These days, cash is king.

What's the scariest thing? Being too young when you come into too much money. If you really do have 200,000 or 300,000 yuan, keep that cash in your hands. Don't give me the line about “what's money for if not to spend?” — anyone who says that has never actually made money.

If you can really earn money, you'll find that as the money grows, you change from the inside out: your thinking, your perspective, how you see the people around you, the energy you give off, your presence, the look in your eyes — all of it changes. The money is there, and so you change. Spend it, and it might look like you've upgraded yourself, like you're driving a nice car — but you haven't actually changed at all.

Someone who has a bit of money and immediately wants to buy a 200,000- or 300,000-yuan car is thinking like a poor person — someone who's been poor so long they just want to prove something: look how well I'm doing. But real money in the bank — whether you put it into value investing, into improving yourself, or just leave it sitting there — beats buying a depreciating car every time.

Spend that much on a car and what you're really buying isn't a car. Poor-person thinking is buying something to prove yourself. But have you ever stopped to ask: prove yourself to whom? Are those people really worth that price?

Your classmates graduated and scattered to the winds — they only exist online now, popping up at the occasional reunion. Your coworkers? Change jobs and you won't know each other anymore. Friends and relatives back home? Could you even make money working in a small county town for two or three thousand yuan a month? You had to go to a big city, to where the money is. And once you're there, the people back home matter a lot less.

Nobody respects you more because of the car you drive. What they respond to is the feeling you give off — that different energy that comes from inside you. And behind that energy is your cash, your confidence, your job, your place in society, your own ability. Those things can't be taken away. And the foundation of all of them is simple: you need to actually have something in your hands. For kids from ordinary families with no resources and no connections, the thing that lets you stand tall is very simple — the number in your bank account, and a self that keeps getting stronger.

Don't Touch Motorcycles — E-Bikes Are the Way

Buy a 100,000-yuan car and drive it back home — will people look up to you? The ones who are better off will still outshine you, and the rich families will still buy their sons 300,000-yuan cars. What exactly did you buy?

But spend five or six thousand yuan on an e-bike, upgrade it the way I described — Michelin tires and all — and it's a completely different story.

As for motorcycles, my advice is: don't touch them. Don't brag to me about motorcycles — there's nothing to brag about. Gas bikes burn fuel, and within the gas-bike world there's a whole pecking order, big bikes looking down on small ones. It's pointless. And in the end it's broken arms and broken legs — some riders even lose the ability to have children, because a motorcycle has a big fuel tank right in front of you, and in a crash or a rear-end collision it slams straight into you. Electric motorcycles are even worse — no point at all. Some young daredevils ride them flat out, 0 to 100 with no gear at all: no helmet, no riding jacket, not even a motorcycle license. They're playing with their lives.

And legally speaking, an electric motorcycle and an e-bike are two completely different things. An electric motorcycle on the road is a motor vehicle — same as a car. Hit someone and you're paying. But on an e-bike, you're the vulnerable party in traffic: if there's an accident, injuries, or damage to pay for, you're almost always the one receiving the money. So electric motorcycles and e-bikes are not the same thing at all.

Of course, e-bikes have strict limits too. The biggest battery you can realistically buy — a 48V 30Ah lithium pack — is about right, with a range of 70 to 100 kilometers. That's plenty.

Conclusion

So for most kids from ordinary families — just starting out, just earning a little money, with parents who didn't have an easy time putting that money together — what car should you actually buy first? The one most worth buying? Go study e-bikes.

Right now, the most enjoyable, the freest, and the best value for money is still the e-bike.
excerpt_en: Saved up a hundred or two hundred thousand yuan and eyeing a Tesla or a Xiaomi SU7? A high-end e-bike — and cash left in the bank — buys you far more freedom than a car loan ever will.
title_en: Young People, Don't Rush to Buy a Car: Your First Vehicle Should Be an E-Bike
